metaDescription: Four sherpa fleece blankets compared on stated gram weights, throw versus queen sizes, texture, shedding and washing, with plain notes on what listings omit.
expertTake: The best all-round pick is the tufted cable jacquard throw, because it states the weight of both layers and adds texture to a plain sofa. The heavy pick is the queen-size blanket with a stated combined weight. Skip a sherpa blanket if you dislike loose fibres, because every synthetic pile sheds a little in the first washes. Wash a new blanket alone before first use, and measure the sofa or bed before you order. A lint roller is a cheap extra.
introParagraphs: A sherpa blanket pairs a smooth fleece face with a woolly, fleece-lined reverse that imitates sheepskin. It is warm for its weight, quick to dry and cheap compared with natural wool. The common complaints are shedding, static and a surface that mats if it is washed hot. Choosing well comes down to size, weight and how much upkeep you will accept.

This guide compares four sherpa blankets that differ in size, weight and surface: a tufted throw, a striped throw, a heavy queen-size blanket and an oversized boxed throw. We evaluated each from published specifications and patterns in owner feedback, and we say plainly where a listing does not give a figure. Gram weights and award mentions come from the makers. Scores are editorial assessments, not measurements.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 50 by 60 in throw covers the lap and shoulders. A 50 by 70 in throw covers a seated adult with feet. A queen blanket covers a bed. Measure the sofa or bed and decide how you will use the blanket before you pick. A blanket that is too small gets pulled off the shoulders, and one that is too large is hard to wash. If you share a sofa, look for the larger sizes. A queen blanket on a sofa drags on the floor, so keep the sizes for their intended use. Bed blankets are best judged by the bed size they state, while throws are best judged by whether they reach your feet when you sit. Leave a little slack so the blanket can tuck in.

Weight in GSM, grams per square metre, shows how dense a fabric is. The tufted throw states 220 and 250 GSM, and the KAWAHOME states 500 GSM in total. A higher number is warmer and heavier. Many listings do not state a weight at all. Treat any stated gram weight as a manufacturer figure. Weight also changes how a blanket feels: a heavy blanket drapes and holds in warmth, while a light one is easier to move and wash. In a warm bedroom, a very heavy blanket can be too hot. Listings rarely say how the weight was measured, so we use it for comparison only and never as proof of warmth. Heavier blankets also stay put better on a sofa.

Flat sherpa is easy to wash and sheds little. A tufted or shaggy surface looks richer and traps lint and hair. Choose by whether you value the look or low maintenance. Owner feedback patterns commonly mention lint in textured surfaces. A soft brush and a lint roller keep a tufted blanket looking fresh between washes. A smooth surface hides pet hair better than a deep cable pattern, which is worth thinking about before you buy a light colour. Brush the surface in one direction for a neat look.

Most sherpa blankets have a smooth face and a woolly back. The woolly side is warmer against the body. A smooth face is easier to keep free of lint and pet hair. If you share the blanket, the two faces let different people choose. Check which face is the woolly one before you buy. Some owners flip the blanket with the seasons, using the smooth face in spring and the woolly face in deep winter. The woolly face also feels warmer to the touch at first.

Synthetic pile sheds fibres in the first washes and builds static in dry rooms. Wash a new blanket alone and tumble on low. Static is a feature of the fibre, not a defect. A cool first wash removes most loose fibre before you use it daily. A humidifier in a dry room reduces static more than any detergent does. If you notice a lot of fibre in the lint trap, run the blanket through another cool cycle before using it. Static also attracts dust.

Sherpa mats if it is washed hot or dried hot. Wash cool, use a mild detergent and tumble low. Check that your washer can take the size, because heavy and queen blankets need a large drum. Air drying is gentler still, though slower. A heavy blanket may need two drying cycles on low heat. Read the care label on arrival, because instructions differ between makers and a wrong cycle can ruin the pile. Never wring a sherpa blanket, because it stretches the backing.

specDecoder.meaning: Grams per square metre. It shows fabric density, so a higher number means a heavier, warmer layer. It is a density figure, not a warmth rating. Two blankets with the same GSM can feel different if the fibre differs. It is most useful for comparing two blankets of the same type.
specDecoder.watchFor: The KAWAHOME states 500 GSM in total. Most other listings give no gram weight, so a missing figure is not a sign of a poor blanket. Check whether the figure covers one layer or both.

specDecoder.meaning: A synthetic fabric that imitates sheepskin lining, usually polyester. It is warm and dries fast. It is not natural wool, so it does not regulate temperature the way wool does. Fleece and sherpa are both polyester, so the difference is in the pile.
specDecoder.watchFor: It can shed and build static. Heat can flatten the pile.

specDecoder.meaning: A blanket with two different faces, usually fleece and sherpa. You choose the side that faces you. It gives some flexibility between seasons and moods. Both sides are usually polyester.
specDecoder.watchFor: Not every reversible blanket has two equally warm sides. Check which face is the woolly one.

specDecoder.meaning: A woven or tufted raised pattern, here a cable design. It adds texture and a little bulk. It looks like a cable-knit sweater in blanket form. The pattern is part of the fabric, not a print.
specDecoder.watchFor: The grooves collect lint. Brush it with the pile, not against it.

specDecoder.meaning: A blanket with no electric element, wires or controls. Its warmth comes from the fabric alone. It is safe to use around children and pets without a power source. Heated blankets are a different product with different safety rules.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Bedsure striped listing states non-heated. It will not warm itself, so it relies on your body heat.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stated size and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which listings give a size, a weight or a thickness. The UGG states all three and the KAWAHOME and the tufted throw state gram weights. Missing figures count against a pick. A listing that states these figures is easier to compare fairly. We did not guess figures that a listing leaves out.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fabric and surface
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared flat, striped and tufted sherpa. Texture adds look and lint. We could not verify fibre content. Our scores are editorial assessments from the listing text. We could not touch any blanket, so softness claims stay claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Price tier
howWeEvaluated.description: We used relative price tiers from the listings and no dollar figures. Prices change, so we compare tiers only. Tiers are relative, with 1 the cheapest in the group. A tier says where a blanket sits in this group, not what it costs today.

howWeEvaluated.title: Washing and care
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted care advice and the risks of matting. Heavy blankets need a large washer. We did not wash any blanket. Where no advice was visible, we advised a cool wash as a safe default. Care advice in listings is often generic.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We read patterns in owner feedback on shedding, static and thickness. These themes recur across the category. We do not publish ratings or review counts. We treated this as soft evidence only. Owner themes shape the cautions in this guide but never replace the listing detail.

cards.text: Easy to wash, low shedding and quick to dry. It looks plainer and sits flatter on a sofa.

cards.label: Tufted

howToChoose.note: A washable, flat-pile blanket suits pets best. A lint roller is useful on every pile.

howToChoose.note: Prices move, so compare current listings. A cheaper throw is a fair way to test whether sherpa suits you.

maintenance.interval: First wash and every few weeks
maintenance.why: Loose fibres come off in the first washes. A cool cycle protects the pile. Washing alone also stops lint from moving onto other laundry. Use a gentle cycle for a tufted surface. Close any zips or ties first.
High heat mats sherpa and flattens the pile. A low cycle keeps it fluffy. Remove it while still slightly warm and fluff it by hand. A dryer ball helps the pile stay lofty.

A shake removes loose fibres and a soft brush lifts matted pile and cable grooves. Do this outdoors if the blanket is shedding. A soft pet brush works well on matted spots. Short brushing sessions work best.
Softener coats the fibres and can make them clump. A little white vinegar in the rinse is a common alternative. Use a mild detergent instead.
Damp storage causes odour. Keep the blanket in a breathable bag. Make sure the blanket is fully dry before folding. Add a cedar block if you are worried about moths.

faq.a: A blanket with a fleece face and a woolly sherpa back that imitates sheepskin lining. It is usually polyester. Several sizes and textures are common. It is a popular, low-cost alternative to real sheepskin.

Many shed a little in the first washes. Wash a new blanket alone and shake it outdoors. Shaking the blanket outdoors helps. Check the lint trap after the first wash. It usually settles after a few washes.

faq.q: How do I wash a sherpa blanket?
faq.a: Wash cool with a mild detergent, skip fabric softener and tumble on low. Use a large machine for big sizes. Air drying is the gentlest option.

A 50 by 60 in throw covers the lap, 50 by 70 in a seated adult and a queen blanket covers a bed. Measure your sofa or bed if you want a full cover. A throw that reaches your feet is usually the most useful.
They are warm for their weight, though no independent source ranks these blankets for warmth. Warmth depends on thickness and the room. A heavier blanket feels warmer at first.

faq.q: Why does my sherpa blanket have static?
faq.a: Synthetic fibres build static in dry air. A humidifier helps. Keeping the blanket away from other synthetics also reduces it. A damp cloth wiped over the surface also helps. A dryer ball can also help.
